title: TA9-02360
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX is a citizen of the Republic of Equatorial Guinea (Equatorial Guinea), who is claiming refugee protection pursuant to s. 96 and s. 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Act (IRPA).1 Allegations

The claimant alleges that he is a member of the Progress Party since 1992. He alleges that he was detained for two weeks without charge in XXXXXX 1992. He assumed various XXXXXX positions within the party over the following years. In XXXX 2008, he alleges that a Lt. Col within the police informed him that he was being sought by the authorities. He decided to flee by boat to neighboring Cameroon. After one week, he returned to Equatorial Guinea, but to the island where the national capital, Malabo, is located. After eight months there, he obtained a Spanish passport with a photo resembling his features, and travelled to Spain on XXXXXXX, 2008. He remained in Spain for two months, but did not claim asylum there. He travelled to Italy, remaining two days in Rome, before travelling to Canada and claiming asylum upon his arrival at Pearson Airport. He alleges a well-founded fear of persecution for reason of his political opinion. Issues and Determination

The panel determines that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The determinative issues were the credibility of the claimant, the subjective fear of persecution and the personalized risk. The panel's reasons are as follows: Identity

The claimant's identity is evidenced by the documentation disclosed, including the certified copies of his national identity card and driver's license,2 the originals being retained by the Canada Border Services Agency.

Prior to the initial sitting on June 29, 2011, the Division had disclosed documentary evidence related to Spain and Spanish nationality,3 as the claimant was born before Equatorial Guinea declared independence from Spain. At the request of counsel for the claimant, an adjournment was granted due to the late disclosure of this information. During the recess, counsel for the claimant disclosed a communication from the Spanish Consulate General at Toronto, under cover of written submissions.4 After considering counsel's last disclosure, and in light of the direction of the Federal Court of Appeal in the Williams decision,5 the panel finds that the claimant does not have Spanish nationality, and Spain is not therefore a country of reference. The panel is satisfied as to the personal identity of the claimant and that he is a citizen of the Equatorial Guinea and no other country. Credibility and Subjective Fear
The panel finds key aspects of the claimant's testimony not to be credible and that his behavior is not consistent with a subjective fear of persecution.

The claimant alleges that his father was detained for 3 years following the 1995 elections. He testified that, nine years later, his father died from injuries sustained from that period of detention. In support of this allegation, the claimant introduced a death certificate.6 According to the death certificate, his father died at the public jail of XXXXXX. However, neither in his oral testimony nor in his Personal Information Form (PIF)7 did the claimant suggest his father was detained at the time of his death. The panel finds this contradictory evidence undermines the credibility of the claimant.

The claimant said that he was constantly being harassed and under threat of arrest. In support of this allegation he introduced a document dated XXXXXX, 2004, purporting to be an arrest warrant.8 Despite the existence of this document, calling for his arrest and capture, the claimant alleges to have been arrested on two occasions: in XXXX 2005, when he was detained for three days without incident, and again in XXXXX 2007, when he was detained overnight and released. His release by the police is not consistent with his allegations that he is wanted for his political activity in opposition to the government.

According to the claimant's oral and written evidence, he was working at two family businesses in XXXX up until XXXX 2008, in order to support his XXXX wives and XXXXX children. The panel finds it reasonable for the authorities to have found and arrested the claimant since he was living in plain sight at this time. That he was arrested and released on two occasions without incident is not consistent with a person who was of active interest to the authorities due to his political activity. As further evidence of his harassment by the authorities he said he was forced from his employment at the XXXXXXX, where he worked from 2006 to 2007. The panel pointed out that, according to his PIF,9 the period of employment was actually 1993 or 1994 until 1994 or 1995. The claimant explained that he was confused. The panel finds this explanation to be unreasonable. The panel finds more likely than not the claimant sought to embellish the period immediately preceding his departure from the country. The panel draws a further negative inference on the credibility of the claimant.

The claimant alleges that the determinative event that prompted his departure from the country was when a friend, a XXXXXX within the police force, called on him late one night, and showed him a list upon which the claimant's name appeared. He introduced a copy of the list.10 The document instructed the competent authorities not to issue travel or identity documents to the named persons, including the claimant, and not to allow their departure from the country. He said this visit occurred on XXXXX, 2008. The claimant was persuaded to take flight because his police contact informed him that many on the list had already been detained and one was executed. The panel notes that there were handwritten additions to the document, noting the word 'jail' beside many names, and that that one person was assassinated on XXXX, 2008. The panel finds it implausible that the list presented to the claimant in XXXX would have foretold of a murder that took place more than 5 weeks later. The panel gives little probative value to the document, accordingly.

The claimant alleges that night he fled to XXXX in the neighboring Republic of Cameroon. The panel asked if the claimant claimed protection there and he said that he did not do so, because there was a diplomatic mission of Equatorial Guinea in the country and he did not feel safe. The panel gave notice of its specialized knowledge11 and informed the claimant that Cameroon is a signatory to the Convention and has a robust refugee program which grants asylum to tens of thousand of persons. The claimant said that during his time in Cameroon he travelled freely from XXXX to XXXX, the XXXXXXXXXXX, thence to XXXXX, the XXXXXXXXXXXX and back to XXXX. Given his freedom of movement in the country, the panel finds it unreasonable for the claimant not to have availed himself of refugee protection in Cameroon.

The claimant testified that after one week in Cameroon, he decided to return to Equatorial Guinea, to make preparations for his definitive flight to safety. Return to the country of nationality may indicate that a well-founded fear of persecution is lacking where the claimant's conduct is inconsistent with such fear.12 The claimant was already in a safe third country. The panel finds unreasonable for the claimant to return to the country from which he fears persecution in order to make arrangements to leave the country definitively. The claimant explained that he did not return to his hometown of XXXX on the mainland, but rather went to the island where the national capital is located. The panel does not find it reasonable for the claimant, allegedly fearing agents of the state, to return not only to his country but close to where the agents of harm are headquartered. He was able to remain on his relations' farm for eight months without incident.

The claimant eventually obtained a Spanish passport and he posed as the bearer of the passport upon his arrival at Madrid. He was granted admission to Spain but did not seek protection there. When asked why, he replied that it was not safe for nationals of Equatorial Guinea there. The panel does not find this explanation to be reasonable. According to the US Department of State Country Report: The country's laws provide for the granting of asylum or refugee status, and the government has established a system for providing protection to refugees. Potential asylum seekers were effectively able to exercise their right to petition authorities. In a 2009 report, however, the national ombudsman noted that complaints related to irregularities in the handling and reporting of some deportation cases had not declined significantly. Asylum seekers are not automatically rejected solely because of their country of origin. All asylum petitions are reviewed individually, and there is an established appeals process available to petitioners. In practice the government provided protection against the expulsion or return of refugees to countries where their lives or freedom would be threatened on account of their race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion. The Asylum and Subsidiary Protection Law provides protection for up to three years for persons who do not meet the criteria for refugee status but face dangers such as torture or the death penalty if returned to their countries of origin. The law includes gender and sexual orientation as conditions for granting asylum; makes free legal assistance available to asylum seekers; provides a single process for both asylum and subsidiary protection (if asylum is denied, subsidiary protection will be automatically considered); contemplates family reunification for asylum seekers; allows asylum requests to be accepted at an embassy or consulate; and provides for the resettlement of refugees in neighbouring countries in some cases.13

There is no objective evidence before the panel to support the claimant's contention that Spain, a country where he speaks the language, was not a safe place to claim asylum. He said that he did not claim asylum during his two days in Rome, Italy, for the same reason, that there was diplomatic representation of Equatorial Guinea in the country. There is no objective evidence before the panel that Cameroon, Spain or Italy would allow agents of a foreign state free reign to target asylum seekers in their respective jurisdictions.

The panel considered the jurisprudence. In the Ilie decision, the Federal Court held: The tribunal was entitled to consider the applicant's failure to claim refugee status in other countries, and to consider how the applicant's evidence was to be weighed in light of that failure.14

In the decision of Hibo Farah Mohamed and Ardo Abdi Omer v. MCI, the Court held: The Geneva Convention exists for persons who require protection and not to assist persons who simply prefer asylum in one country over another. The Convention and the Immigration Act should be interpreted with the correct purpose in mind.15

Similarly, in the Case of Assadi, Nasser-Eddin v MCI, the Court held: Failure to immediately seek protection can impugn the claimant's credibility, including his or her testimony about events in his country of origin.16

The panel determines that the claimant's failure to seek protection on three separate occasions before arriving in Canada further undermines his credibility as a witness and his subjective fear of persecution.

The panel considered the jurisprudence. In the case of Kamana, the Federal Court held: 'The lack of evidence going to the subjective element of the claim is a fatal flaw which in and of itself warrants dismissal of the claim, since both elements of the refugee definition - subjective and objective - must be met.'17

Likewise in the Geron decision, citing the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in Ward,18 the court held that the lack of evidence going to the subjective element of the claim was a 'fatal flaw'.19 More recently, in the Ahoua decision, the Court held: 'The Minister properly pointed out that a negative finding regarding subjective fear may render the assessment of the objective aspect of the complaint superfluous and may in itself warrant the dismissal of the claim.'20

Finally, the panel considered the medical report. The physician's examination relates to scars allegedly incurred by the claimant during his alleged detention in 1992.21 Given the passage of 16 years from the alleged incident, the panel gives little probative value insofar as motivating the claimant's subjective fear to flee his country in 2008.

After considering the claimant's failure to seek protection in either Cameroon, Spain and Italy, where the claimant had reasonable opportunities in those countries to do so, and his return to the country from which he was seeking persecution, which reasonably could have led to contact with the alleged agents of harm, and the concerns about the credibility of the claimant's evidence, the panel determines that he has not established a subjective fear of persecution. The panel determines, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant is not being sought by state agents for his political beliefs. The panel determines, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant was not politically active in Equatorial Guinea. He is not a Convention refugee, accordingly. Danger of Torture

The claimant did not allege that he feared a danger of torture in Equatorial Guinea. The panel is satisfied on a balance of probabilities that he does not face such a danger. Risk to Life, Cruel and Unusual Treatment or Punishment

The personalized risk, unlike the fear of persecution, does not depend upon the claimant's subjective fear. The documentary evidence establishes that the human rights situation in Equatorial Guinea is appalling.22 However, in light of the foregoing analysis, the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, the claimant has not established a personalized risk. Notwithstanding an allegedly long-standing political involvement in a banned political party, for which he was known to the police, and actively sought for arrest and detention from 2004, the claimant continued his life largely untrammeled until XXXX 2008 and again for 8 months in the vicinity of the national capital from XXXX until XXXXXX 2008.

The panel considered the jurisprudence. In the Prophète decision, later upheld by the Federal Court of Appeal, the Federal Court declared in part: The test under s. 97 of the Act is distinct from the test under section 96. As Rouleau J. noted in Ahmad v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2004 FC 808, [2004] F.C.J. No. 995 (QL), at para. 21, s. 97 "requires the Board to apply a different criterion pertaining to the issue of whether the applicant's removal may or may not expose him personally to the risks and dangers referred to in paragraphs 97(1)(a) and (b) of the Act" and must be assessed with reference to the personal situation of the applicant. Moreover, he indicated that the "assessment of the applicant's fear must be made in concreto, and not from an abstract and general perspective" (at para. 22). Accordingly, documentary evidence which illustrates the systematic and generalized violation of human rights in a given country will not be sufficient to ground a section 97 claim absent proof that might link this general documentary evidence to the applicant's specific circumstances (Ould v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FC 83, [2007] F.C.J. No. 103 (QL), at para. 21; Jarada v. Canada (Minster of Citizenship and Immigration), 2005 FC 409, [2005] F.C.J. No. 506 (QL), at para. 28; Ahmad, supra, at para. 22).23

After considering the claimant's testimony and the documentary evidence, the panel determines that any risk the claimant faces is one shared generally by other persons in Equatorial Guinea at this time. He is not a person in need of protection, accordingly. Conclusion

The claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The panel therefore rejects his claim. (signed) "Michael S. McCaffrey" Michael S.
